doc.title: Joe Ascione interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Breakthrough with Billy Mitchell at Sonny's Jazz Club
summary: Charlie Perry pointed him to tenor player Billy Mitchell. At Sonny's on Long Island Mitchell told him 'you're the drummer, play the drums' and hired him for twelve years of Wednesdays.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: When was the first, what you would consider to be a breakthrough job for you?

Okay, this one always comes to mind. When I was young studying with Charlie Perry, I was about seventeen, he always mentioned the tenor player Billy Mitchell, not the other Billy Mitchell, the tenor player Billy Mitchell with the Basie band. I think he was with Basie, what ’57 to ’61 give or take. But he lives on Long Island and I always knew of him. I think he replaced Buddy Tate at the time if I’m not mistaken.

So I always knew of him and Charlie Perry always used to say see if you can get to hook up with Billy. It never happened until a couple of years later, Sonny’s Jazz Club on Long Island had Billy do a Wednesday night steady gig for a while. And somehow I got the call from Sonny, the owner. And he said, “Hey, Joe” real raspy voice, scotch-ladened voice, you know “Joey, baby, come on here and play with Billy.” And I was nervous. So I’m sitting there and it’s I think Wes Belcamp and Pete Chivoli who used to play with Stan Kenton for a while, Wes is a good piano player. Mark Elf, guitarist, and I’m sure there were other — Bill Easley might have come down and Frank Wess came down, a lot of those guys live out on Long Island. So I was there and I’m just, not wanting to keep it safe, but wanting to do the gig. So the first set goes by and no one attacked me, I didn’t attack anyone. Things are good. I’m outside, I see Billy outside smoking, and mustered up the courage and I said, “Billy, I don’t know what you’re looking for, do you have any suggestions? Loud? Soft? Sticks? Brushes?” So he looks at me and he says, “You’re the

drummer, play the drums.” All right. So I walk in the house, in the place, scratching my head. I see Mark Elf, you’re the drummer, play the drums. I say, “Mark, what the hell’s this guy talking about? You’re the drummer, play the drums?” He said, “Man you can’t kick those tubs hard enough.” He said, “He’s played with Blakey and Elvin and Buddy Rich” and this and this. He said, “Just go, man, hit ‘em.” All right. Next set so I boom- boom, start bashing. “Yeah, yeah, all right.” And by the end of that set he turned around and he said, “From now on you’re my drummer.” And I did like twelve years of Wednesday nights at Sonny’s Jazz Club. So to me I think of that as a breakthrough for someone like a Billy Mitchell to be that excited musically. So that was great. And it was a good confidence builder too. So I say to myself well I can play with Billy Mitchell, he’s okay with it, so let me venture out even more. So I would say that was a pivot point.
